summary_html: Case results in **child fatality or serious injury**, triggering mandatory federal and state review. Data and lessons inform systemic reform.
authority_html:
- **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** — establishes national commission and reporting requirements  
- **CAPTA §5106a(b)(2)(A)(x)** — mandates public disclosure and case review of fatalities

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: Termination of the father's rights to his surviving son was affirmed on the cruel-or-abusive-conduct ground after clear and convincing evidence showed he was the sole caretaker when his five-week-old daughter sustained the fatal non-accidental injuries.
key_cases.relevance: This is the Rhode Island decision showing how a child fatality is used to terminate rights to a surviving sibling.
key_cases.quote: the statute dictates that "the department has no obligation to engage in reasonable efforts to preserve and reunify a family."

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: Rhode Island DCYF social workers were entitled to qualified immunity on substantive due process claims by twins abused in foster care because the evidence did not show conscience-shocking conduct, and Rhode Island sovereign and qualified immunity barred the state negligence claims.
key_cases.relevance: Serious injury to a child in DCYF foster care does not itself establish liability; the plaintiff must prove the workers knew of and ignored the danger.
key_cases.quote: state officials must have been at least aware of known or likely injuries or abuse and have chosen to ignore the danger to the child

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on a child protection agency to protect a child from private violence, so the county's failure to remove Joshua DeShaney from his abusive father was not a constitutional deprivation.
key_cases.relevance: When a child dies or is seriously injured after DCYF had contact with the family but had not taken custody, DeShaney is the threshold obstacle to any federal damages claim.
key_cases.quote: But nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors.

key_cases.holding: Abuse and neglect findings were affirmed on medical evidence of fourteen non-accidental fractures, and the mother's Fourteenth Amendment challenge to DCYF's seventy-two-hour hold was not preserved because the parents waived the Rule 15(c)(5) probable-cause hearing.
key_cases.relevance: Serious non-accidental injury to an infant is the fact pattern that drives both the hold and the adjudication here.
key_cases.quote: Therefore, we conclude that Kimberly's challenge to the temporary hold on the children was not preserved for appeal.

key_cases.holding: Termination of the father's rights to Jazlyn was affirmed on the cruel-or-abusive-conduct ground, the Court holding that abuse of another child in the household, together with medical evidence of inflicted injury to Jazlyn, supported the finding.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Rhode Island decision establishing that catastrophic harm to one child in a household is the evidentiary foundation for protective action as to a surviving sibling.
key_cases.quote: cruel or abusive conduct towards one child in a household can serve as a basis for terminating a parent's rights with respect to another child in the household

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: Dismissal of the section 1983 claims arising from the murder of a teenage state witness in Providence was affirmed because the state's unkept promises of protection did not deprive her of liberty, so neither the special-relationship nor the state-created-danger theory removed the case from DeShaney.
key_cases.relevance: When a child or youth is harmed after state actors knew of the danger but never took custody, Rivera is the decision that forecloses the damages claim absent a genuine deprivation of liberty.
key_cases.quote: Merely alleging state actions which render the individual more vulnerable to harm, under a theory of state created danger, cannot be used as an end run around DeShaney's core holding.
